title: Dry Lease vs Wet Lease Aircarft Legal Differences
subtitle: Dry Lease vs Wet Lease
content:
Choosing an aircraft arrangement is not simply a question of whether an operator needs an aircraft, a crew, or temporary capacity. The structure can affect who has operational control, which certificate and operating rules apply, and how maintenance, insurance, liability, and regulatory risk are allocated.

Schedule a consultation with Aero Law Center or call (954) 869-8950 before signing an aircraft lease.

The key dry lease vs wet lease aircraft legal differences are operational control and the services supplied with the aircraft: a dry lease generally provides the aircraft without crew. A wet lease supplies the aircraft and at least one crew member. ACMI arrangements typically package the aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance. The parties’ actual responsibilities and the full contract determine the legal and FAA analysis. FAA guidance treats operational control as a matter of legal responsibility.

For Part 135 operators, air carriers, aircraft owners, and other aviation businesses, labels alone do not resolve the analysis. Before signing, the parties should test the proposed arrangement against the facts of performance, certificate authority, and contract language. That review starts with what a dry lease actually transfers and what the lessee must control. An aircraft transaction attorney can help evaluate those issues alongside the commercial terms.

What Is a Dry Lease in Aviation and How Does It Work?
A dry lease generally separates the aircraft asset from the operation of the aircraft. The lessor provides possession of the aircraft under a lease, while the lessee assumes the operational responsibilities defined by the agreement and applicable regulations. The arrangement may support a Part 91 operation or another business structure, but the label alone does not determine the legal result.

Operational control is the central issue
For a lessee, the most important question is who has operational control: the legal responsibility for initiating, conducting, and terminating a flight. FAA guidance explains that operational control is a matter of legal responsibility, not the size of the aircraft or the number of aircraft in a fleet. The parties should therefore assign that responsibility clearly rather than relying on informal practices or a lease title.

In a typical dry-lease structure, the lessee must understand how crew arrangements fit within that allocation. The agreement should identify who selects, employs, contracts with, trains, and directs any crew used for the operation. If a management company assists with pilot procurement, training, scheduling, maintenance, fuel, or related services, those services should be documented without obscuring which party retains operational control. An FAA legal interpretation addressing these management functions illustrates why the details of the relationship matter.

Maintenance, airworthiness responsibilities, insurance, indemnity, and possession also require precise drafting. The lease should state who performs or arranges maintenance and who bears the associated costs. It should identify required insurance, when risk transfers, and how the aircraft is delivered, inspected, returned, or repossessed. Address records, defects, downtime, and compliance duties for the intended operation as well.

FAA guidance is designed to help lessees avoid agreements that fail to maintain operational control with the appropriate party. Before signing, aviation businesses should compare the written terms with the actual flow of money, personnel, scheduling, maintenance, and flight decisions. Aero Law Center’s Part 91 dry lease operational control resource provides additional context for that diligence.

What Is a Wet Lease and When Do Operators Use It?
A wet lease generally involves an aircraft supplied with at least one crew member by the lessor. That differs from a dry lease, where the aircraft is supplied without crew. This practical distinction is useful, but it does not by itself answer the legal or regulatory questions in a proposed arrangement. Operators and certificate holders must examine who controls the flight, provides the crew, directs scheduling, accepts responsibility for compliance, and holds the relevant authority.

When a wet lease may fit an operator’s needs
A wet lease can help an air carrier or charter operator add capacity without immediately sourcing and integrating every operational resource internally. For example, an operator may consider the structure when it needs aircraft and qualified crew for a defined period, seasonal demand, or a particular route or customer requirement. The commercial convenience does not eliminate the need to document the arrangement carefully.

Federal rules define an air carrier to include a person that undertakes air transportation directly by lease or another arrangement. The parties should not assume that the lessor’s involvement removes the lessee’s regulatory responsibilities. Federal guidance also states that wet leasing from an individual or entity not separately authorized to engage in common carriage can be contrary to federal aviation regulations. The authorization, certificate status, and actual roles of both parties require review before operations begin.

The agreement should address operational control in terms that match the parties’ conduct. FAA guidance treats operational control as a matter of legal responsibility. An FAA interpretation has considered how management services, pilot procurement, maintenance, training, and scheduling interact with a purported dry lease. Those factors can matter when evaluating whether a transaction functions as represented, regardless of the label placed on the document.

For operators comparing dry lease vs wet lease aircraft legal differences, the key question is not simply who supplies the aircraft or crew. It is whether the full arrangement, including side agreements and day-to-day practices, aligns with the applicable certificate, operating rules, and allocation of responsibility. Classification is fact-dependent, so counsel should review the complete structure before execution.

Whether it’s aircraft transactions, commercial litigation, or compliance, we excel at creating solutions to unique challenges.

What Is an ACMI Lease, and How Is It Different?
An ACMI lease is a commercial arrangement in which one party supplies an aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance. The name comes from those four components: Aircraft, Crew, Maintenance, and Insurance. In practical terms, an ACMI arrangement can give an operator access to lift and operating support without requiring the operator to provide every resource itself.

Why ACMI Is Often Compared With a Wet Lease
Because the lessor generally provides the aircraft and crew, ACMI is often described as a form of wet-lease or wet-lease-like capacity. That shorthand can be useful, but it does not answer the legal questions that matter before signing. The agreement should identify who operates the aircraft, who exercises operational control, which party holds the applicable certificate, and how maintenance, insurance, scheduling, dispatch, and regulatory responsibilities are allocated.

The FAA treats operational control as a matter of legal responsibility, not aircraft size or fleet size. Its guidance is intended to help lessees avoid agreements in which operational control is not clearly maintained by the appropriate party. See FAA guidance on operational control and aircraft leasing.

That is why an ACMI label should not be treated as a complete legal classification. The contract, the parties’ certificate status, and their actual conduct can affect how the arrangement is evaluated. A package that looks like a capacity solution may still raise questions about commercial operations and common carriage, including whether the parties are performing the roles described in their documents.

The distinction from a dry lease is also practical. In a dry lease, the lessee typically provides its own crew and assumes the operating responsibilities assigned to it. In an ACMI arrangement, the supplied crew and bundled services may leave the lessor or another authorized operator responsible for significant operating functions. The allocation must be reviewed against the intended operation, applicable FAA rules, and the parties’ real-world practices. No universal conclusion follows from the word ACMI alone.

Key Dry Lease vs Wet Lease Aircraft Legal Differences
The commercial label is only the starting point. The agreement should show who has operational control, who supplies personnel and services, and who bears responsibility when an operation fails. Industry terminology generally treats a dry lease as an aircraft supplied without crew and a wet lease as an aircraft supplied with at least one crew member. FAA legal guidance describes these distinctions, but they do not determine the legal result by themselves.

At a glance: The table below summarizes typical responsibilities. The parties’ contract, certificate status, and actual conduct control the legal analysis.

Typical allocation of responsibilities in dry lease, wet lease, and ACMI structures
Issue	Dry lease	Wet lease	ACMI
Operational control	Usually rests with the lessee, subject to the full facts and agreement.	Often remains with the provider, but the parties’ actual conduct matters.	Commonly structured as provider-operated capacity, subject to regulatory and contractual review.
Crew and maintenance	Lessee generally arranges crew and assumes stated maintenance duties.	Provider supplies the aircraft and at least one crew member; responsibilities must be allocated precisely.	Provider packages aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance.
Payment and possession	Often a fixed lease payment with possession transferred to the lessee.	Payment may reflect aircraft and operating services, without the same possession model.	Payment commonly covers agreed capacity or hours, while possession and service scope remain contract questions.
Liability and risk	Lessee may carry substantial operational, insurance, and indemnity obligations.	Provider may retain operating responsibilities, but liability, delay, and indemnity terms require close review.	Risk is divided across the bundled services and must be matched to actual control and performance.
Why the allocation matters
Operational control is a question of legal responsibility, not aircraft size or fleet size, according to FAA guidance. The agreement should therefore identify who directs flights, selects and controls crew, controls scheduling, handles maintenance decisions, and accepts regulatory responsibility. Payment terms, possession, insurance, and indemnities should support that allocation rather than contradict it.

A dry lease can still create risk when a management company supplies pilots, schedules flights, or performs other services in a way that blurs the lessee’s control. The FAA has addressed arrangements involving management, pilot procurement, maintenance, training, scheduling, and dry leasing, so those functions should be documented carefully. A wet lease or ACMI structure also requires diligence regarding the provider’s authority, the scope of services, and applicable operating rules.

Misclassification risk is serious. The FAA warns that devious leases and conditional sales contracts can disguise operations subject to Parts 121, 125, or 135. The parties should evaluate the substance of the arrangement, not rely on its title.

Question and answer
What is the main legal difference between a dry lease and a wet lease? A dry lease typically supplies the aircraft without crew, while a wet lease supplies the aircraft with at least one crew member. The controlling legal question is who bears operational control and related regulatory responsibility under the actual arrangement.

How Do Dry Lease vs Wet Lease Aircraft Legal Differences Affect FAA Review?
The FAA analysis does not end with the label in the contract. Regulators may examine who has operational control, who provides the crew, who makes scheduling and dispatch decisions, and whether the arrangement effectively provides air transportation. Those facts can affect whether Part 91, 121, 125, or 135 rules apply, and whether the parties hold the authority required for the operation.

Operational control, truth-in-leasing, and sham-lease risk
FAA Advisory Circular 91-37B describes operational control as a matter of legal responsibility, not aircraft size or fleet size. A lease should therefore identify the responsible party with precision and align the contract with actual conduct. A nominal dry lease may create risk if the lessor, management company, or another party continues to control crew selection, scheduling, dispatch, maintenance decisions, or other operational functions. The FAA has specifically warned that devious leases and conditional sales contracts can disguise operations subject to Parts 121, 125, and 135.

Truth-in-leasing documentation and related delivery requirements should be reviewed alongside the operating agreement, management agreement, and actual practices. An FAA legal interpretation also addresses arrangements involving maintenance, pilot procurement, training, fuel, scheduling, and catering while an aircraft is described as dry leased. The facts should be evaluated as a complete operating model, not in isolated contract clauses. See the FAA guidance in AC 91-37B and the FAA interpretation at FAA legal interpretation 13611.

For additional context, review Aero Law Center’s guide to FAA operator classification and compliance before assuming a proposed structure fits a particular operating rule.

Certificates, wet-lease authorization, and operations specifications
Part 1 defines an air carrier to include a person undertaking air transportation directly by lease or another arrangement. The practical question is therefore whether the transaction creates, supports, or masks an air-carrier or commercial-operator activity. A provider engaging in charter air service generally must hold the applicable FAA certificate, and the certificate holder’s operations specifications may control what aircraft, routes, services, and wet-lease arrangements are authorized.

Wet leasing deserves separate diligence. Federal Register wet-lease policy guidance states that an air carrier wet leasing an aircraft from an individual or entity not separately authorized to engage in common carriage is contrary to the Federal Aviation Regulations. The parties should confirm the lessor’s authority, the lessee’s certificate status, required approvals, and any applicable operations-specification provisions. Review 14 CFR Part 1, 14 CFR 119.53, the FAA material at FAA media 13716, and the Federal Register wet-lease policy guidance. Operators should also confirm their Part 135 certification requirements where applicable.

Schedule a consultation with Aero Law Center or call (954) 869-8950 before signing. The regulatory result is fact-dependent and should be confirmed by aviation counsel.

What an Aviation Attorney Reviews Before You Sign an Aircraft Lease
Before an operator signs, counsel should test whether the written deal matches the proposed operation. The FAA treats operational control as a question of legal responsibility, not aircraft size or fleet size. Its guidance is intended to help lessees avoid agreements that leave that responsibility unclear. The contract also must work under applicable state contract law, which can affect remedies, indemnities, payment disputes, and enforcement.

Pre-signing diligence for aviation operators
For Part 135 operators and air carriers, the review should address the following checkpoints:

Parties and authority. Confirm each lessor, lessee, owner, manager, and affiliate is correctly identified, authorized to contract, and able to convey the stated rights. Check title, liens, corporate authority, and any required owner or lender consent.
Operational control. State who has final authority and responsibility for initiating, conducting, and terminating each flight. Avoid language that assigns responsibility to one party while another party actually controls scheduling, dispatch, crew, or flight decisions.
Crew and management separation. Identify who selects, employs, trains, supervises, and pays the crew. If a management company supplies pilots, scheduling, or other services, review whether the combined arrangement remains consistent with the intended operating rules.
Maintenance and airworthiness. Allocate inspections, records, discrepancies, repairs, parts, return-to-service decisions, and continuing airworthiness duties. Confirm that responsibility is practical, not merely nominal.
Insurance and indemnity. Match insurance requirements to the operation, name additional insured parties accurately, and define indemnity triggers, exclusions, defense obligations, and liability limits.
Payment and possession. Specify rent, reserves, taxes, fees, delivery conditions, acceptance, aircraft use restrictions, and when possession and risk transfer.
Governing law. Separate federal FAA compliance questions from state-law contract provisions. A choice-of-law clause does not replace required federal approvals or operating authority.
Regulatory approvals. Confirm certificates, operations specifications, authorizations, registrations, and required notices before operations begin. The intended label cannot cure a structure that functions differently.
Exit and default. Address maintenance defaults, grounding, late payment, repossession, termination, transition of passengers and records, casualty, insolvency, and post-termination cooperation.
Aircraft leasing is part of Aero Law Center’s aircraft transaction practice. Operators evaluating these issues can review the firm’s aircraft lease legal considerations resource, then obtain advice tailored to the aircraft, certificate status, counterparties, and proposed operation.

Frequently Asked Questions
What are the main legal differences between a dry lease, wet lease, and ACMI arrangement?
A dry lease generally provides the aircraft without a supplied crew, while a wet lease provides the aircraft with at least one crew member. ACMI usually packages the aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance, but the label does not decide the legal result. The full agreement, actual services, possession, and operational-control responsibilities must be reviewed together.

Who has operational control under a dry lease?
That depends on the agreement and the parties’ actual conduct. The lessee may assume operational control in a legitimate dry-lease structure, but management, scheduling, maintenance, pilot procurement, and related services can affect the analysis. FAA guidance treats operational control as a matter of legal responsibility, not fleet size, and warns lessees to assign it clearly. FAA Advisory Circular AC 91-37B

Does a wet lease automatically authorize commercial charter operations?
No. A wet lease does not replace the certificate or authorization required for the operation. The FAA states that legitimate charter air service requires an applicable Part 121, 125, or 135 certificate. While federal guidance addresses limits on wet leasing from an entity not separately authorized for common carriage. Federal Register wet-lease policy guidance

What should an operator verify before signing an ACMI agreement?
Confirm which party controls flights, supplies and supervises crew, performs or arranges maintenance, carries insurance, holds required certificates, and bears regulatory responsibility. Also review possession, payment, indemnities, records, operational specifications, default rights, and exit terms. An ACMI structure can solve a capacity need while still creating material compliance and contract exposure if those responsibilities are unclear.

Schedule a Consultation Before You Sign
Lease labels do not resolve every operational-control, FAA, or contract question. A focused review can help your team evaluate how the proposed dry lease, wet lease, or ACMI arrangement assigns responsibilities and manages regulatory exposure before execution. title: Ariworhiness Certificate Requirements Aircarft Owner Guide
subtitle: Airworthiness Certification
content:
An airworthiness certificate is more than paperwork stored in an aircraft’s records. It is part of the legal foundation for operating, buying, selling, and managing an aircraft, and its significance continues beyond the date it is issued.

For an aircraft owner, airworthiness certificate requirements aircraft owner obligations generally center on maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition, complying with applicable FAA rules, and preserving the records that support continued operation. The certificate authorizes flight, but it does not replace the owner’s or operator’s continuing responsibility under the regulations. See the FAA’s airworthiness certificate guidance for the federal framework.

That distinction matters when maintenance, airworthiness directives, modifications, or a transaction raises questions about what the certificate proves and what it does not. The starting point is understanding exactly what the FAA certificate legally certifies.

Ready to discuss an airworthiness certificate issue? Call Aero Law Center at (954) 869-8950 to request a consultation.

Aero Law Center services aviation businesses globally for all of your aviation business needs.

(954) 869-8950
Start Your Free Consultation Today
What Is an Airworthiness Certificate and What Does It Legally Certify?
An airworthiness certificate is an FAA document that authorizes an aircraft to operate in flight. It is not merely an ownership document or a general statement that an aircraft is safe under every circumstance. The certificate reflects the aircraft’s eligibility for operation within an approved design, category, and applicable operating requirements. The FAA regulates issuance under 14 CFR Subpart H.

A registered aircraft owner or the owner’s agent may apply. The basic process requires registration, an application, and an FAA determination that the aircraft is eligible and in a condition for safe operation. Applicants generally submit the request through the FAA Airworthiness Certification tool or use Form 8130-6 through the appropriate FAA servicing office. The certificate itself may be issued only by an FAA Aviation Safety Inspector or an authorized representative of the Administrator.

For an owner or operator, the legal significance is practical. Operating rules generally require a civil aircraft to carry an appropriate and current airworthiness certificate, subject to specific regulatory exceptions. The certificate must also be available for the required display. Those requirements should be considered alongside the broader FAA certificate compliance requirements that apply to the aircraft’s operation and business structure.

Most importantly, possessing a certificate does not eliminate the continuing obligation to keep the aircraft airworthy. A certificate and a current airworthy condition are related, but they are not identical. Maintenance, alterations, records, operating limitations, and applicable FAA requirements can affect whether a particular flight is lawful and safe. The precise analysis depends on the aircraft, its certification category, its operation, and the facts in its records.

Standard vs Special Airworthiness Certificates: Key Differences
The certificate classification affects the aircraft’s approved category, permitted purpose, and the records an owner or operator must keep current. The label alone does not establish unrestricted operating authority. The aircraft’s category, configuration, operating limitations, and applicable FAA rules still control.

title: FAA Part 145  Repare STation Certification Requiremnts
subtitle: FAA Part 145
content:
For an aviation maintenance business, pursuing FAA certification is more than completing an application. The station must be prepared to show that its people, facilities, equipment, technical data, manuals, and quality processes support the work it intends to perform.

Schedule a Consultation about your Part 145 certification or compliance needs, or call (954) 869-8950.

The faa part 145 repair station certification requirements begin with an FAA-acceptable application and extend to the repair station’s ratings, housing and facilities, management structure, training program, and inspection readiness. The exact scope depends on the ratings and operations requested, so a generic checklist is not a substitute for a careful review of the proposed station.

Understanding what the certificate authorizes, and how ratings and operations shape that authorization, provides the right foundation for evaluating the certification path and the compliance responsibilities that follow.

Aero Law Center services aviation businesses globally for all of your aviation business needs.

(954) 869-8950
Start Your Free Consultation Today
What Is a Part 145 Repair Station and Why Does FAA Certification Matter?
A Part 145 repair station is an aviation maintenance business that holds an FAA certificate authorizing specified maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alteration work within defined limits. Certification is not a general endorsement for every service an MRO may want to offer. Under 14 CFR 145.53, a station qualifies for a certificate with appropriate ratings and operations specifications when it meets the applicable requirements of Part 145, Subparts A through E. Those operations specifications prescribe the station’s authorized operations and limitations, with safety as the governing concern.

For an MRO evaluating the faa part 145 repair station certification requirements, the practical question is whether its people and facilities support the intended work. Tools, technical data, procedures, and management structure must also align. The certificate creates the regulatory framework, but the ratings and operations specifications define the meaningful scope of the business.

Ratings define the maintenance scope
Part 145 rating categories include airframe, powerplant, propeller, radio, and instrument ratings. A station’s rating is therefore not merely a designation for marketing materials. It is tied to the types of articles and work the station is approved to handle. An MRO should align its proposed services, capability planning, equipment, personnel qualifications, and technical data with the ratings and limitations reflected in its FAA authorization.

That alignment matters when the business expands, changes its service model, or accepts work that falls near the edge of its approved capability. A certificate does not eliminate the need to evaluate the specific article, task, data, and authorization involved in each maintenance job.

Accountable management supports controlled operations
Certification also depends on a functioning management system, not just a compliant facility. The application must identify the repair station’s organizational structure and the names and titles of managing and supervisory personnel. In operation, the repair station manual must identify management positions, areas of responsibility, and the duties and authority assigned to those positions. This structure helps connect executive accountability with daily decisions about quality, records, personnel, and return-to-service processes.

For a station building or maintaining its compliance program, the broader Part 145 maintenance compliance framework can help place certification obligations in the context of ongoing FAA regulatory work. The legal and operational analysis remains fact-specific, particularly when ratings, operations specifications, facility changes, contractors, or customer requirements are involved.

FAA Part 145 Repair Station Certification Requirements and Approval Process
FAA certification is best treated as a sequenced readiness process, not a single form submission. FAA guidance identifies five phases: preapplication, formal application, design assessment, performance assessment, and administrative functions. Each phase gives the applicant an opportunity to align its proposed ratings, procedures, people, facilities, and records before the FAA evaluates the station’s ability to operate within its requested scope.

Preapplication. Begin by defining the proposed certification scope and preparing for contact with the FAA certification team. The FAA lists Form 8400-6, Preapplication Statement of Intent, among the forms associated with Part 145 certification. Applicants should use the preapplication phase to identify the information and documentation needed for the proposed repair station rather than treating the process as an informal commitment to approval. FAA Part 145 forms provide the agency’s listed forms and descriptions.
Formal application. The application must be submitted in a format acceptable to the FAA. The package includes an FAA-acceptable repair station manual, an FAA-acceptable quality control manual, the station’s organizational chart, and the names and titles of managing and supervisory personnel. It also describes the housing and facilities, including the physical address, and includes a training program for FAA approval. Form 8310-3, Application for Repair Station Certificate and/or Rating, is listed by the FAA for this purpose.
Prepare management and eligibility documentation. FAA guidance states that key management personnel should attend the formal application meeting with the certification team. A corporate applicant must provide its state Certificate of Incorporation and accompanying documentation needed for the FAA to evaluate eligibility. If the applicant seeks to perform maintenance functions on air-carrier or commuter aircraft or components, it must also provide a drug and alcohol program for FAA approval.
Design assessment. During this phase, the FAA evaluates whether the proposed manuals, organization, training program, facilities, equipment, personnel, and technical data are designed to support the requested certificate and ratings. The application should therefore describe an operating system that can be implemented, not merely an intended future state.
Performance assessment and administrative functions. The applicant must be prepared to demonstrate that its proposed system works as represented. Required equipment, personnel, technical data, housing, and facilities must be in place for FAA inspection when the certificate or rating is approved. The final administrative phase follows the FAA’s evaluation of the application and demonstrated performance. The FAA’s process guidance should be used alongside the applicable regulations and the station’s specific facts; it does not guarantee approval or establish a universal timeline.
Early legal and compliance review can help identify gaps between the application package, corporate structure, proposed scope, and operating reality before those gaps become certification obstacles.

Whether it’s aircraft transactions, commercial litigation, or compliance, we excel at creating solutions to unique challenges.

Start Your Free Consultation Today
What Ratings, Facilities, and Tools Must a Repair Station Have?
A Part 145 certificate does not authorize every type of maintenance. The station’s ratings, facilities, equipment, materials, and technical data must align with the work it is approved to perform. That alignment should be treated as an operational control, not simply an application detail. The applicable rules also require the relevant equipment, personnel, technical data, housing, and facilities to be in place for FAA inspection when a certificate or rating is approved.

title: 14 CFR Part 43 Maintenace Compliance Requirements
subtitle: Maintenace Compliance Requirements
content:
For an aviation operator or maintenance, repair, and overhaul business, 14 CFR Part 43 maintenance compliance requirements are the working rules behind aircraft maintenance. They address maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, alteration, return to service, records, life-limited parts, performance standards, inspections, and airworthiness limitations.

Schedule a consultation with an aviation attorney to discuss a Part 43 compliance concern, an FAA inquiry, or a maintenance-related business risk.

This article focuses on the compliance and legal obligations that matter to aircraft operators, certificate holders, Part 145 repair stations, and MRO leadership. It is not a substitute for reviewing the current regulation, an aircraft’s approved data, applicable operations specifications, or the facts of a particular maintenance event. For the broader relationship between operator classification and FAA obligations, see Aero Law Center’s FAA regulatory compliance and operator classification guide.

Aero Law Center services aviation businesses globally for all of your aviation business needs.

(954) 869-8950
Start Your Free Consultation Today
14 CFR Part 43 Maintenance Compliance Requirements for MROs
14 CFR Part 43 is the Federal Aviation Administration’s maintenance rule. Under section 43.1, it generally governs maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alteration of aircraft with a U.S. airworthiness certificate. As well as certain foreign-registered civil aircraft used in common carriage or carriage of mail under Parts 121 or 135. It also applies to the airframe, aircraft engines, propellers, appliances, and component parts covered by the rule.

The current eCFR text is the controlling starting point for determining scope. It also identifies limited exceptions, including certain experimental aircraft and aircraft operated under Part 107, subject to the regulation’s stated conditions. That means a company should not treat a general summary of Part 43 as a universal answer. The aircraft’s certificate, operation, maintenance program, component, and applicable operating rules all matter.

Part 43 matters because maintenance work is not complete merely when a technician finishes the physical task. The work must be performed by an authorized person, in accordance with applicable performance rules and approved or acceptable data. It must be documented in the required form and approved for return to service by a person with the required authority. A failure in any one of those steps can create operational, enforcement, contractual, insurance, or litigation exposure.

Who Must Follow FAR Part 43 Maintenance Requirements?
Part 43 obligations can reach several roles in an aviation business. The precise duties depend on the work performed and the regulatory framework governing the aircraft or operation.

The compliance analysis commonly includes:

Aircraft owners and operators: They must ensure required maintenance is completed and records are preserved. They must also avoid operating an aircraft when it is not in an airworthy condition or when required maintenance documentation is missing.
Maintenance personnel: A person performing maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration must fall within the authorization rules and perform the work in a manner consistent with Part 43.
Persons approving return to service: Section 43.7 addresses who may approve an aircraft, airframe, engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service after covered work.
Part 145 repair stations and MROs: A repair station must consider both Part 43 requirements and the separate privileges, ratings, procedures, records, quality controls, and limitations that apply under Part 145.
Air carriers and commercial operators: Parts 121 and 135 contain additional maintenance-program and inspection requirements. Part 43 still matters, but it does not replace those more specific operational rules.
A useful internal control is to identify, before work begins, who is performing each task and what authority permits that person to perform it. Identify who will approve return to service, what technical data controls the work, and what record entry is required. When a business cannot answer those questions consistently, the problem is often a process and governance issue rather than a single technician issue.

What Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alteration Does Part 43 Govern?
Part 43 separates several types of work that can have different authorization and recordkeeping consequences. Maintenance generally includes inspection, overhaul, repair, preservation, and replacement of parts, but the correct classification depends on the work and the regulatory definitions that apply. Preventive maintenance is a limited category of simpler tasks listed in Appendix A. Rebuilding and alteration involve their own requirements, including the treatment of major repairs and major alterations.

Appendix A is especially important for businesses assessing whether work qualifies as preventive maintenance. A task should not be treated as preventive maintenance simply because it appears routine, inexpensive, or familiar. The person performing the work must still be authorized, the task must fit the applicable list and conditions, and the work must be recorded and approved as required.

For major repairs and major alterations, Appendix A and Appendix B should be reviewed together with the approved or acceptable technical data. Depending on the work, a Form 337 or another required record may be involved. The fact that a modification is physically small does not, by itself, determine whether it is a major alteration. Classification should be made using the applicable regulatory criteria and technical context.

Part 43 also contains performance rules in section 43.13. In general terms, maintenance must use methods, techniques, and practices acceptable to the FAA and must use materials and tools that are appropriate for the work. The aircraft or product must be returned to a condition for safe operation, and the work must account for the manufacturer’s maintenance instructions and other applicable data. A compliance review should therefore connect the task card, work order, manuals, parts documentation, inspection steps, and final approval rather than treating each record as an isolated form.

What Are the Preventive Maintenance Requirements Under Part 43?
Preventive maintenance under Part 43 is limited maintenance that may be performed by a person authorized under the applicable rule. Including a pilot-owner in circumstances allowed by the regulation. The task must be one of the preventive maintenance items listed in Appendix A, and the person performing the work must follow the applicable instructions, limitations, and recordkeeping requirements.

Before returning an aircraft to service after preventive maintenance, the responsible person should confirm:

The task is actually within the preventive maintenance list and is not a repair, alteration, or inspection requiring a different authorization.
The person performing the task is authorized to perform it on that aircraft and under that operating context.
The work was completed using the appropriate methods, techniques, practices, materials, tools, and technical data.
The required maintenance record entry identifies the work, date of completion, person who performed it, and person approving return to service when the rules require separate approval.
Any operational or airworthiness limitations, inspection requirements, or related discrepancies have been addressed before the aircraft is operated.
For a repair station or MRO. Preventive maintenance questions may arise when a customer asks the facility to perform work that appears simple but falls outside the facility’s authorized process or the definition in Appendix A. Escalating an uncertain classification before work begins is generally safer than trying to correct an incomplete record after delivery.

Part 43 Recordkeeping Requirements: What Must Operators Document?
Recordkeeping is one of the most important parts of Part 43 compliance because the record is often the evidence that the work was properly performed and approved. Section 43.9 addresses the content, form, and disposition of maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alteration records. Subject to the inspection-related provisions that have separate treatment under section 43.11 and other referenced rules.

A typical maintenance record entry should be specific enough to show what was done and how the aircraft or product was returned to service. Depending on the work, the record may need to identify the date, a description or reference to acceptable data. The name of the person performing the work, the signature or approved identifier, and the approval for return to service. A vague entry such as “work completed” may not provide a defensible record of the actual maintenance.

Operators and MROs should also maintain a controlled process for several records tasks:

Link work orders, task cards, inspection findings, and parts traceability to the final maintenance entry.
Identify life-limited parts and preserve the information needed to establish their status.
Record major repairs and alterations in the form and manner required by Part 43.
Protect electronic records from unauthorized alteration, loss, or destruction.
Retain records for the period required by the applicable rule, operating specification, maintenance program, or contract.
Correct an error transparently rather than overwriting, backdating, or obscuring the original record.
The FAA’s AC 43-9D provides information about maintenance recordkeeping and FAA Form 8130-3. The FAA describes the circular as guidance, not as an independent source of legally binding obligations. And notes that it does not apply in the same way to air carrier maintenance programs under specified Parts 121 and 135 provisions. Use it as a compliance aid alongside the regulation and the operator’s approved programs, not as a replacement for them.

How Do Return-to-Service and Inspection Rules Affect Compliance?
Return to service is a regulatory approval, not merely a statement that a mechanic believes the task is finished. Section 43.5 addresses approval for return to service, and section 43.7 identifies persons who may provide that approval for the relevant aircraft or component. The approval should correspond to the work actually performed and the authority held by the approving person.

Inspection work may trigger additional requirements. Section 43.11 addresses the content, form, and disposition of records for certain inspections conducted under Parts 91 and 125 and specified Part 135 provisions. The applicable inspection program, aircraft category, and operating rules determine which record format and approval language is required.

For an MRO, a sound release process should keep several actions separate:

Completion of a maintenance task.
Completion of an inspection or required functional check.
Correction of a discrepancy.
Approval for return to service.
Delivery of the aircraft or component to the customer.
Separating those steps helps management identify who made each decision and what evidence supports it. It also creates a clearer response if an operator later receives an FAA request, a customer claim, or a question about whether the work met the applicable requirements.

Common Part 43 Compliance Problems and FAA Enforcement Risk
Part 43 problems often arise from process breakdowns rather than a single dramatic event. Common risk areas include:

Performing work outside the authority, rating, or procedure available to the person or facility.
Using technical data that is not applicable, current, or acceptable for the work.
Failing to identify whether a repair or alteration is major.
Omitting required information from a maintenance or inspection record.
Approving return to service without completing the required inspection or discrepancy resolution.
Losing traceability for life-limited parts or parts installed during maintenance.
Altering, reproducing, backdating, or falsifying a maintenance record.
Allowing customer pressure, production targets, or a rushed aircraft release to override a documented stop-work process.
Section 43.12 specifically addresses maintenance records involving falsification, reproduction, or alteration. Depending on the facts, a Part 43 issue may also affect an operator’s airworthiness determination, operations specifications, certificate status, customer contracts, insurance position, or exposure to civil claims. The legal consequences depend on the evidence, the applicable operating rules, the seriousness of the conduct, and the FAA’s enforcement posture.

If the FAA raises a concern, preserve the relevant work orders, records, personnel authorizations, training materials, manuals, parts documentation, communications, and quality-system records. Avoid making an unsupported admission or changing historical records without a controlled legal and technical process. Frequently Asked Questions About Part 43 Compliance
What are the requirements for preventive maintenance under CFR Part 43?
Preventive maintenance must fit the applicable list in Appendix A, be performed by a person authorized under the applicable rule. Follow the required methods and limitations, and be recorded and approved for return to service as required. A routine task is not automatically preventive maintenance.

What is required under FAR Part 43 before returning an aircraft to service?
The covered maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, alteration, or inspection must be completed using applicable requirements and acceptable methods. The required record must be made, and a person authorized under section 43.7 must approve return to service when the rule requires that approval.

Does Part 43 apply to a Part 145 repair station?
Part 43 requirements commonly apply to maintenance work performed by or for a Part 145 repair station. While Part 145 adds separate certification, rating, facility, personnel, quality, and procedural requirements. A repair station should evaluate both parts and any applicable approved procedures or operating limitations.

What should an MRO do after discovering a maintenance record error?
Secure the original record and related work evidence, stop any process that could compound the error, involve the appropriate maintenance and quality personnel. And obtain legal guidance when the issue may affect airworthiness, an FAA report, a customer dispute, or potential enforcement. Do not silently overwrite or backdate a historical record.
